Round 94b: four ways to mix two fonts

Your question: "Is there a way we can do a mix of two fonts?" Yes, four ways, each shown with fonts from round 94's board (codes as there). The pairs are examples of each technique, not picks: any two of the board's fonts can go through any of them.

1. Two fonts, two jobs

The most common mix: one face for the name, another for everything around it (the store text, the game's UI, the object names). Each stays whole; the pair is the identity.

2. One word, two faces

Most letters from one face and a few from another, baseline and cap height matched. The medieval version is the illuminated initial; the logo version is one letter that carries the idea.

3. Layered

Both faces whole, stacked: one as a shadow, a ghost or an inner light behind or inside the other. Colour separates them.

4. A true blend

Every letter's outline moved part of the way from one face to the other, so the result is a new face between them (done here by merging each letter's strokes, sampling both outlines and interpolating). Faces built alike blend cleanly at every step: Cormorant SC into Cinzel Decorative. Faces built differently hold together only at small amounts: around 15-30% a Garamond takes on a gothic tension, and by 50% the shapes stop agreeing (the P's bowl, the blackletter's extra strokes have no partner). A blended wordmark is usually redrawn by hand from the step that works. Grenze Gotisch is this idea made properly by its designers: a face on the border between roman and blackletter.
